transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Owen Mills (Redwood Solutions), Samir Rao (Asterix VP Eng), Lena Ortiz (Asterix SRE), Marcus Chen (Asterix Security)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on private/VPC onramp for Redwood Private deployment. Main concerns: egress IPs, region gating (EU vs US), peering vs PrivateLink style endpoints, and audit/KMS integration. Customer wants a pilot in us-west-2 then expand to eu-central-1 with strict residency.

Topics:
- VPC peering vs transit gateway options
- Private endpoint models (AWS PrivateLink vs internal NAT)
- Egress IP stability and allowlisting for downstream APIs
- Regional deployment strategy and data residency
- Security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jamie Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time today. Just to orient, this is a kickoff to talk about Asterix's private onramp needs and egress constraints. Nina and I will cover connectivity options and call out common patterns.
[00:12] Samir Rao: Great, thanks. We're mainly trying to understand how Redwood would deploy inside our VPCs and what we need to open on our side. We're evaluating hosted and dedicated too but this call is private-first.
[00:25] Nina Patel: Awesome. We usually start with two patterns: direct VPC peering/transit gateway or private endpoint model where Redwood exposes private endpoints into your VPC. Each has tradeoffs for IP management and region routing.
[00:40] Lena Ortiz: Quick q: we have strict egress allowlists for downstream partners, so we need stable egress IPs or a predictable NAT for requests hitting external APIs. How does Redwood handle that?
[00:52] Owen Mills: Short answer: for Redwood Private we can either route egress through a customer-managed NAT inside their VPC or we can provide fixed egress CIDR ranges if you're using Redwood-managed egress via a transit gateway. It's config dependent.
[01:10] Marcus Chen: When you say fixed ranges, are those static? Our security policy says we can only allowlist static IPv4s, ideally a /28 or smaller. Dynamic pools won't pass audit.
[01:23] Nina Patel: We can allocate stable egress IPs per customer in the managed scenario — usually a small pool — but if you need absolute determinism, customer-managed NAT is the cleanest: you terminate egress inside your VPC and control the public IP.
[01:38] Samir Rao: Ok that helps. Next, region gating: GDPR, we need model inference for EU customers to stay in eu-central-1. Can Redwood pin model execution regionally?
[01:51] Jamie Carter: Yes — Redwood Private supports region pinning. You can pin workloads to a region or set routing policies so EU traffic stays in eu-central-1. For Hosted we'd do routing via region-specific endpoints, but for Private it's straightforward since you control the VPCs.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: Any caveats switching between regions? Like KV cache replication or model shard syncing? We run low-latency inference for chat.
[02:16] Nina Patel: Good question. For stateful sessions we rely on KV cache locality; cross-region sync adds latency. For multi-region active/active we recommend per-region model replicas with async replication for logs/metrics. We can design session affinity to keep tokens local.
[02:33] Marcus Chen: From security: what's the key management story? We require envelope encryption with customer KMS.
[02:41] Owen Mills: We support customer KMS integration for model payloads and storage. For private deployments we can integrate with your KMS via IAM roles and the runtime uses envelope keys. We'll include an HSM option for enterprise plans.
[02:55] Samir Rao: Are audit logs and request traces available to our SIEM? Need to forward logs to our ELK stack.
[03:03] Nina Patel: Yup, audit logs, per-request traces, and token-level cost/latency are exportable. We can ship via S3 + Kinesis or push to your SIEM over VPC peered endpoints. We'll share our log schema.
[03:17] [crosstalk] Lena Ortiz: Sorry, just — how intrusive is the peering? We prefer to avoid broad route propagation if possible.
[03:25] Jamie Carter: We commonly use Transit Gateway with route maps to restrict propagation, or direct VPC peering for simpler use-cases. If you want to avoid bringing in routes, PrivateLink style private endpoints are least invasive: only the service ENIs show up.
[03:40] Samir Rao: Hmm reminder: our infra team prefers not to manage a separate NAT for cost reasons, but security demands stable egress. Tradeoff.
[03:50] Marcus Chen: Also curious about IP whitelisting to third parties. If Redwood egress IPs are used, will they be shared across tenants?
[03:58] Nina Patel: In our managed pools we can dedicate CIDR blocks per enterprise customer; for multi-tenant hosted, IPs are shared. Private deployments give the most isolation.
[04:09] Samir Rao: Good. Let's talk throughput: baseline 2k requests per second, peaks 5k rps. Mostly short context windows but some long session tails. Any guidance on instance sizing and network bandwidth?
[04:23] Owen Mills: We'll run short benchmarks but ballpark: for 2k rps with small models you need at least two dedicated GPU pods with high bandwidth NICs and a fronting autoscaler for spikes. For 5k, we recommend sharding across regions and using batching with sub-50ms tail SLOs. We'll size it in the follow-up.
[04:40] Lena Ortiz: Are there known issues with bursty traffic and our egress costs? Bursts can spike NAT throughput.
[04:48] Nina Patel: Yes bursts can increase NAT and transfer costs. We typically put egress-heavy calls through a caching layer or separate worker pool that has predictable egress patterns. We'll show patterns we've seen in similar customers.
[05:00] Samir Rao: What about private endpoint DNS? We enforce split-horizon DNS.
[05:06] Jamie Carter: We support custom DNS via VPC resolver rules. If you use PrivateLink, you get hosted zone names and we hand over the private IPs; for peering you can use your internal DNS to map endpoints.
[05:18] Marcus Chen: Any client-side certs or mTLS? For sensitive calls we need mutual auth.
[05:23] Nina Patel: mTLS is supported for control plane and we can enable mTLS for specific ingestion endpoints. Data plane can also use mTLS; we'll include cert rotation recommendations.
[05:35] Samir Rao: There was a reference to KV cache earlier — can someone explain the cache behavior in a then multi-region context?
[05:42] Nina Patel: The runtime keeps token caches per node. For lowest latency you colocate requests to the same region. We can do sticky routing and prefix caching to reduce cold starts. In multi-region you'd have replica caches, with async sync for telemetry only. Some terms in the transcript may be misheard like K-V cash or cache spelled different, apologies for transcript quirks.
[05:58] Lena Ortiz: Switching to compliance: we need SOC2 + ISO27001 docs and penetration test reports. Can Redwood provide those?
[06:05] Jamie Carter: Absolutely — we'll send SOC2 Type II and ISO summaries and an up-to-date pen test redacted report. Also we have a PCI note for customers that need it.
[06:15] Owen Mills: Also add that for Private deploys we can run on customer's account which aligns with your compliance posture; or we can use a dedicated account model with cross-account roles.
[06:27] Samir Rao: Timeline: we'd like a pilot by end of August — is that feasible?
[06:33] Nina Patel: Feasible. Typical pilot timeline: 2–4 weeks of network prep and peering, then 2 weeks of validation and perf runs. So starting network work mid-July gets you into an August pilot.
[06:45] Lena Ortiz: Ok we'll need a checklist for our network team.
[06:48] Jamie Carter: We'll send a peering + private endpoints checklist and a short runbook for NAT/egress configs.
[06:55] [10:15] Samir Rao: Quick question — any limitations on supported cloud services in the VPC? For example our data store talks to a managed cache that uses private endpoints. Will Redwood traffic touch that?
[10:25] Nina Patel: If you peer, Redwood can call into your private services if policies allow. If you use PrivateLink, we only see what you explicitly expose via endpoint, so it's safer. There are also IAM role options for cross-account access if Redwood needs to pull artifacts.
[10:40] Marcus Chen: How about logging retention inside our VPC? We want to retain request logs for 1 year — is that supported without shipping to your storage?
[10:48] Owen Mills: You can choose to keep logs in your account S3 and we will forward them; retention is then under your control. If logs are stored in Redwood managed storage, retention follows our plan but we can arrange longer retention for enterprise.
[11:00] Samir Rao: Any networking gotchas like AWS limit on ENIs if using PrivateLink at scale?
[11:06] Nina Patel: Good callout. PrivateLink creates ENIs per AZ per endpoint. For high-scale multi-AZ usage we often recommend Transit Gateway or direct peering to avoid ENI limits. We'll include AZ-level guidance in the checklist.
[11:20] Lena Ortiz: On certs and SSO — we use Okta with SAML. How does Redwood handle SSO for the console and audit log access?
[11:27] Jamie Carter: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. For Private deployments we can federate into your IdP so all access is managed by Okta.
[11:37] Samir Rao: Are there any examples of customers doing EU-only model execution? I want a reference architecture.
[11:43] Nina Patel: Yes, we have a couple of finance customers in EU. We'll send a short reference architecture doc that shows per-region model replicas, private endpoints, and cross-region metrics flow.
[11:54] [17:02] Marcus Chen: Let's talk about cost. If we choose managed egress vs customer NAT, how does cost attribution work? We need predictable billback to product teams.
[17:11] Owen Mills: We can break out egress and compute usage by tenant and export detailed token-level cost data. If we manage egress, we include egress charges and show line items; if you manage NAT, egress is on your bill and compute is on ours.
[17:24] Samir Rao: Good. Also curious about fallback strategies if a region is degraded. Does Redwood auto-failover to another region? That impacts residency though.
[17:33] Nina Patel: We have routing policies that can failover to a compatible region or model variant. For regulatory constrained traffic we can disable auto-failover and instead use a degraded mode that returns a controlled error or fallback to a smaller model in-region.
[17:46] Lena Ortiz: Is there a way to test failover without impacting production?
[17:51] Jamie Carter: Yes, we can do canary tests and simulate region failover in a staging environment. We'll include a playbook for that.
[18:00] Samir Rao: Ok, final item: procurement and legal — we need data processing addendum (DPA) and standard enterprise contract redlines.
[18:07] Owen Mills: We'll loop in legal. Jamie will send the standard DPA and a sample SOW for Private deployment.
[18:15] [25:00] Samir Rao: Do you support private peering across cloud providers? We have resources in GCP and AWS and prefer a single private plane.
[25:09] Nina Patel: Cross-cloud private connectivity is trickier; we can use customer transit (e.g., Equinix Fabric) or VPN mesh. Redwood Private can be deployed in multiple clouds and tied together via your transit; we don't force intercloud traffic unless explicitly configured.
[25:26] Marcus Chen: Any special notes on IPsec/VPN latencies if we use that for cross cloud?
[25:32] Nina Patel: IPsec often adds ~10–50ms overhead — depends on tunnel throughput and CPU offload. For tight latency SLOs we prefer colocated regional deployments instead of cross-cloud calls.
[25:45] Lena Ortiz: One thing — we use an egress proxy that does TLS inspect. Does that break anything?
[25:51] Jamie Carter: TLS inspection can break mTLS. If your proxy does intercept, you may need to exempt Redwood flows or use a dedicated outbound path that preserves mTLS. We'll document the header and cert expectations.
[26:05] Samir Rao: This is super helpful. Can you put together a short architecture doc + checklist and timeline we can share with procurement?
[26:13] Jamie Carter: Absolutely — we'll share those. Expect an email with links to: network checklist, SOC2/ISO docs, sample peering configs, and a proposed pilot timeline.
[26:25] [Wrap-up]
[26:30] Jamie Carter: Recap: Action items — Jamie sends diagrams and security pack; Lena gives egress IPs; Nina does sizing; schedule deep-dive week of 7/13. Pilot target: end of August. Is everyone aligned?
[26:45] Samir Rao: Yep aligned. Thanks.
[26:48] Marcus Chen: Thanks all.
[26:50] Lena Ortiz: Thanks.
[26:52] Nina Patel: Thanks, will follow up.
